newsitem.title: UK: EIU sees world wheat price fall by end-1996.
newsitem.headline: EIU sees world wheat price fall by end-1996.

text.p: World wheat export prices are likely to fall to around $160 per tonne for US No 2 hard winter fob Gulf by the end of the year from around $180 per tonne in September, the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) said.

Barley is seen steady but could drop on a good 1997 EU harvest and maize (corn) may edge up early next year before slipping again. EIU forecasts were contained in its World Commodity Forecast-Food, Feedstuffs and Beverages for the fourth quarter of 1996.
The EIU predicted an erratic course for wheat prices in the new year, with levels hitting $190 per tonne in the second quarter of 1997.
"If the USA or other major producers are hit by drought in the second quarter of 1997 prices could go far above $200 per tonne," the EIU said.
But assuming that supplies improve again in 1997-98, prices will fall and selective subsidisation could bring them to around $150 per tonne for some customers, the EIU said.

Markets have tumbled as harvest prospects improved in the major exporting countries, but the EIU reckoned swings in market sentiment seem out of proportion with the modest changes in the fundamentals, "which still point to the continuation of a tight market until at least 1998," it said.
The EIU expects barley export prices, on the basis of French barley fob Atlantic ports, to range between $140 and $160 per tonne until mid-1997.

Barley prices were at $150 per tonne in August and lower in early September, the EIU said. Assuming another good EU harvest they could then move down to the $130-$150 per tonne range. Maize (corn) prices could rise to $170 per tonne in the first half of 1997, from about $150 in September, the EIU said.
Maize is seen dropping to $140 per tonne later in 1997 then recovering to around $160 by mid-1998.

The EIU based its forecasts on US No 2 Yellow corn fob Gulf, but says that white maize for human consumption will probably trade at similar levels "assuming a reasonable South African crop." --Christopher Lyddon, London newsroom +44 171 542 7928
